strengths: Tackles a novel and challenging inverse problem: recovering dynamic internal muscle deformation from surface observations, extending digital humans beyond surface-only parametric models.

Introduces SKIM, a multi-view marker-based dataset with synchronized RGB, ArUco marker tracks, ground-truth poses, canonical skin/muscle/skeleton meshes, and marker-to-muscle bindings, which can support future work.
Proposes a concrete learning pipeline combining decoupled non-linear blendshapes for muscle and skin layers with biomechanically inspired regularizers.
The regularization design, including area-normalized smoothness, bending resistance, stretching, tangential sliding, and volume preservation, is technically well motivated and clearly described.
Reports improvements over kinematic LBS and an adapted HIT baseline on some metrics, especially extreme surface errors, intersection ratios, and subcutaneous volume preservation.
Includes ablations of architecture and regularization choices, and acknowledges several limitations and future directions.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle deformation is not directly validated: there is no dynamic internal ground-truth muscle data. Training only uses sparse surface marker residuals, so the predicted muscle layer is largely unobserved and prior-driven; anatomical plausibility metrics do not establish anatomical correctness.

The internal anatomical template is obtained from static heuristic volumetric fitting rather than personalized medical imaging. Errors in this template are not quantified and can propagate to all downstream muscle predictions.

The evaluation metrics are proxies for plausibility rather than accuracy. Low intersection and preserved volume can be achieved without matching true internal muscle motion, and no metric evaluates individual muscle shape or activation accuracy against ground truth.

Quantitative gains are mixed: the full model has worse global MPME than the LBS baseline (13.43 mm vs. 13.11 mm) and similar intersection ratios. Much of the improvement in volume preservation appears to come from handcrafted regularizers rather than learned muscle dynamics.

The ablation shows Linear, MLP, and U-Net architectures perform similarly, weakening the evidence that the proposed learned model is necessary or captures non-linear muscle behavior beyond simple surface fitting.

The acquisition setup is expensive and person-specific, requiring a custom ArUco suit, a 120-camera mocap studio, and a 140-camera scanner. The claim of a scalable and cost-effective solution is therefore overstated for practical deployment.
The baselines are limited. HIT is a static internal-tissue estimator adapted to SMPL, not a dynamic muscle baseline, and there is no comparison to FEM or medical-imaging-based dynamic ground truth.

Dataset documentation is insufficient: only five subjects, no demographic/consent/ethics details, no clear benchmark split or evaluation protocol in the main paper, and no repository link despite claiming data and code are available.

The method assumes ground-truth skeletal pose and a marker suit during training, and remains subject-specific. It does not address robustness to pose estimation error or markerless inference, which limits real-world impact.

Some presentation and citation issues remain, e.g., Table 1's reference to Kemper et al. appears mismatched, and key reproducibility details such as hyperparameters, training runtime, and implementation specifics are largely deferred to supplementary material.

strengths: Targets an important and challenging inverse problem: estimating internal muscle deformation from external surface observations, which is a novel direction for vision-based human modeling.

Introduces SKIM, a multi-view marker-suit capture with canonical marker-to-muscle correspondences, skeletal poses, residual fields, and visibility masks; such data could be valuable if released and properly documented.

The method combines person-specific non-linear blendshapes with several biomechanically inspired regularizers (smoothness, stretching, tangential sliding, volume preservation), and the paper attempts to validate physical plausibility via volume and intersection metrics.
Qualitative visualizations and an interactive viewer illustrate plausible muscle bulging and per-muscle querying, suggesting feasibility of the concept.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle deformation is not directly validated. No ground-truth internal muscle imaging, such as MRI, CT, or ultrasound, or simulated muscle ground truth is used; the muscle anatomy comes from a separate volumetric fitting method, so the paper only tests marker tracking and proxy physical metrics, not muscle accuracy.

Despite claims of scalability and cost-effectiveness, the capture requires 120-camera mocap, a 140-camera scanner, a custom marker suit, and per-subject templates. The experiments use ground-truth skeletal poses, not poses estimated from RGB video, so the from-video and arbitrary-motion claims are not supported.

Baseline evaluation is weak and possibly unfair. Only LBS and static HIT are compared; no pose-corrective body models, learned soft-tissue methods, or biomechanical or FEM comparisons are included. HIT is a static estimator evaluated cross-topology, and its large tracking error may reflect the mapping rather than its own quality.

Quantitative results are mixed and marginal. The method is worse than LBS in MPME, intersection is identical to LBS, and deep muscle volume error of 10.35 percent is much higher than HIT's reported 1.95 percent; the justification for this tradeoff is qualitative and lacks ground truth. No error bars, per-subject statistics, or significance tests are provided.

The method is explicitly subject-specific, trained separately per subject, and evaluated on only five subjects. It therefore does not constitute a generalizable parametric model and offers limited scalability or broad impact as claimed.

Reproducibility is insufficient. Critical details such as marker tracking post-processing, seam handling, volume derivation, binding mechanism, metric definitions, train and test splits, and baseline configurations are relegated to supplementary material. No actual dataset or code link is provided despite the data and code available claim.

Technical novelty is moderate. The architecture is a standard U-Net or MLP or linear blendshape model; the ablation shows architecture choice is not critical, and regularization mainly affects volume metrics with only small tracking gains. The main novelty lies in the capture and data, but that dataset is small and not demonstrably accessible.

Clarity and presentation issues remain: missing subsection numbering, notation inconsistencies, and overclaims such as anatomically grounded with real data and first method that are not adequately supported by the presented evidence.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel inverse problem and application area: inferring subject-specific dynamic muscle deformation from surface observations, rather than only modeling the visible skin or simulating internal anatomy with expensive FEM. This is a timely and high-impact direction for biomechanical digital humans.

The SKIM dataset is a substantial contribution: it couples a custom marker-embedded suit, multi-view RGB capture, high-resolution body scans, canonical skin/bone/muscle meshes, marker-to-muscle correspondences, ground-truth skeletal poses, and sparse residual deformation fields. Such data is rare and valuable for future work on anatomy-aware human modeling.

The SOMA architecture is technically reasonable: decoupling muscle and skin deformation into cascaded non-linear blendshapes is a sensible way to model structural muscle volume and sliding skin residuals, and the canonical residual supervision removes global pose dependence from the data term.

The biomechanically inspired regularization is thoughtfully designed: smoothness, bending resistance, stretch preservation, tangential anchoring, and volume preservation are motivated and implemented with care. Using canonical and posed volume constraints to counteract LBS candy-wrapper collapse is an elegant idea.

The experimental evaluation, while proxy-based, is broader than a simple proof of concept: it compares against LBS and HIT, includes tracking metrics, high-error percentiles, interpenetration proxies, volume-preservation proxies, and ablations over architecture and regularization terms. The method improves MedPME/P90 and substantially reduces large dynamic-region errors compared with LBS.

The paper is generally clear, well illustrated, and candid about limitations. Code and data are stated to be available, and the real-time Viser visualization strengthens the practical potential of the framework.
weaknesses: The central scientific claim, recovering internal muscle deformations, is not directly validated against dynamic in-vivo muscle ground truth. Supervision comes only from sparse skin-surface markers; internal muscle motion is inferred through regularizers and a static volumetric template. The reported volume and interpenetration metrics are useful proxies, but they do not demonstrate that the recovered muscle shapes are anatomically correct during motion.

The muscle/skin disentanglement is fundamentally underconstrained. Because only the sum D_skin = D_musc + D_res is supervised by marker residuals, the network can explain surface observations with many different splits between muscle and skin. Hand-crafted priors reduce implausible solutions, but they cannot guarantee that the muscle layer captures true muscle behavior rather than a plausible-looking decomposition.

Individual muscle prediction appears to be mostly a passive transfer: the global muscle layer is learned, and individual muscles are animated by barycentric binding from that boundary layer. This is useful for visualization but weaker than modeling per-muscle deformation, so the claim of targeting individual muscles is not fully supported by the method or quantitative evaluation.

The framework is person-specific and requires a heavy acquisition pipeline: a custom marker suit, a 120-camera mocap studio, a 140-camera body scanner, and volumetric anatomical fitting. This conflicts with the framing of a scalable, cost-effective, RGB-based solution; the limitations acknowledge this, but the practical accessibility remains far from markerless in-the-wild capture.

The quantitative comparisons are not fully convincing as a validation of internal anatomy. HIT is a static internal-tissue estimator and not a dynamic muscle-deformation baseline, while cross-topology comparisons require barycentric mapping that may disadvantage the baseline. The intersection ratio for Ours is essentially identical to LBS in Table 2, so the claim of strictly avoiding interpenetration is not directly evidenced by the tabulated numbers alone.

Several important details are deferred to supplementary material or are missing from the main paper: network/training specifics, dataset splits, hyperparameter sensitivity, subject count, consent/privacy handling, and statistical variability. There are also minor clarity/attribution issues, such as the apparent mismatch between 'Kemper et al. [8]' in Table 1 and the reference entry, and section numbering gaps (4.1.3/4.1.4 without 4.1.1/4.1.2).

The ablation improvements in global tracking are modest (e.g., full model 13.43 mm vs. w/o physics 13.71 mm), and the deep muscle-to-bone volume error remains 10.35%, which is not negligible. The paper explains this as a compromise to avoid collisions, but it also indicates that the internal volumetric accuracy is still limited.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: recovering internal muscle deformation from external surface observations (multi-view RGB + marker suit) is an interesting, under-explored inverse problem in vision, distinct from surface-only human models and non-scalable FEM approaches.

The SKIM dataset is a substantial, non-trivial resource: 5 subjects, ~45 min each, 120-camera studio, dense ArUco suit (~2310 markers), ground-truth skeleton, tracked 3D marker trajectories, residual fields, and per-vertex bindings. Releasing it with code and an interactive Viser tool strengthens reproducibility and downstream utility.

The decoupled muscle/skin blendshape formulation with hand-designed biomechanical regularizers (smoothness, biharmonic bending, stretch, tangential sliding, signed-prism volume preservation) is thoughtfully constructed and each prior is ablated, showing measurable improvements in tracking error and volume preservation.

Ablation studies (architecture, vector regularization, physical energies) are reasonably thorough and support the design choices; the signed-volume formulation elegantly penalizes geometric inversions via negative volumes.

Clear pipeline: canonical template construction, marker-to-muscle ray-based binding, barycentric binding of individual high-res muscles, and canonical-space residual supervision that yields pose-invariant training.

Honest discussion of limitations (subject-specificity, dependence on volumetric fitting initialization, marker-suit requirement, lack of force/co-contraction modeling, lack of in-vivo dynamic volumetric GT).
weaknesses: Fundamental validation gap: there is no ground-truth internal anatomy during motion, so the actual accuracy of the recovered muscle shapes is never verified. All reported metrics (marker tracking error, intersection ratio, volume preservation) are surrogates that can be satisfied without producing anatomically correct muscles. The claim of 'anatomically grounded' recovery is therefore weaker than the title and abstract suggest.

The system is explicitly per-subject: each subject requires a separately trained U-Net for the skin/muscle layers. This contradicts the standard meaning of a 'parametric model' and limits the impact considerably; the paper is essentially five subject-specific regressors plus a shared template construction pipeline. Generalization is not demonstrated.

The 'individual muscle' prediction is not truly independent prediction: high-res muscle meshes are obtained by barycentric propagation of the aggregate boundary-layer displacement (Eq. 14). Thus individual muscles cannot express different behaviors from each other, which weakens the central claim that the method 'targets individual muscles'.

Baseline comparisons are weak and possibly unfair. HIT is mapped through SMPL and reports an MPME of 115.34 mm (P90 = 354.80 mm), which is implausibly large and more likely reflects a registration/topology mismatch than the intrinsic failure of the method; such a comparison does not provide a meaningful reference point. No comparison is made against FEM-based or other anatomically-informed learned models (e.g., Komaritzan et al., Wenninger et al., Han et al.), which the related-work section itself identifies as closest competitors.

The reported 'improvements' are marginal in places: MPME is 13.43 (Ours) vs 13.11 (LBS), i.e., a modest degradation on the mean, and the deep muscle volume error of 10.35% (M→B) remains large; the paper's narrative glosses over this as a 'realistic physical compromise' without external evidence.

The biomechanical priors are regularizers rather than physics: terms like bending resistance, edge-stretch, and volume preservation do not enforce actual muscle force generation, activation, or PCSA physics. The framing as 'biomechanically inspired priors' risks over-selling their biological fidelity.

Dependence on initialization: templates are produced by volumetric fitting (Komaritzan et al.), and the method cannot correct errors in that initialization; since the anatomical ground truth is inherited, downstream errors and any bias in the fitting are propagated into the learned dynamics without being quantified.

The motivation of 'scalable and cost-effective' is partially undercut by the pipeline's heavy machinery: 120-camera capture, custom suit, manual UV-seam marker annotation, and per-subject training. These practical limitations are acknowledged but not reflected in the impact claims.

strengths: Addresses an important and difficult inverse problem: inferring internal muscle deformation from accessible multi-view RGB/surface observations rather than medical imaging.

Introduces the SKIM dataset, which combines multi-view RGB, dense ArUco marker tracking, ground-truth skeletal pose, subject-specific skin/muscle/bone meshes, and residual deformation fields for five subjects.

The technical pipeline is detailed, including canonical marker correspondence, multi-view triangulation/refinement, LBS-based residual computation, pose-space U-Nets, and biomechanically inspired regularizers.
The quantitative evaluation reports improvements over LBS and HIT in dynamic tracking errors and interpenetration, and the ablation studies examine architecture and regularization choices.
The physics-inspired energies (smoothness, bending, stretch, tangential sliding, volume preservation) are thoughtfully designed and ablated, showing effects on plausibility metrics.
Data and code are claimed to be available, and the supplementary material provides substantial implementation and dataset details.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle anatomy is not validated against ground-truth dynamic internal muscle geometry. Internal muscles are obtained from volumetric fitting [33] on static scans, not from MRI/CT or another true 3D ground-truth source, so the model could produce plausible but anatomically incorrect muscle motion.

The muscle layer is only indirectly supervised through skin marker residuals: Eq. 7/8 supervise D_skin, not D_musc. The decomposition D_skin = D_musc + D_res is ambiguous, and the network could explain surface residuals largely through D_res while D_musc remains regularized but not anatomically correct.

The claimed ability to target individual muscles is overstated. The high-resolution individual muscles are deformed by barycentric transfer from one global muscle boundary layer, so they are not independently simulated or supervised; they largely move in synchrony with that single layer.

The method relies on volumetric fitting [33] for the anatomical template, even though the paper criticizes heuristic/template-based anatomy transfer for being visually plausible but anatomically inaccurate. This undermines the 'anatomically grounded' claim and is acknowledged only as an initialization limitation.

Evaluation metrics are mostly plausibility proxies (volume preservation, intersection ratio, tracking error), not direct measures of muscle shape accuracy. Table 2 even shows HIT achieving lower M->B volume error (1.95% vs. 10.35%), so the evidence for superior internal anatomy is mixed.

Baseline comparisons may not be fully fair: HIT is evaluated via a generic SMPL template, while SOMA uses subject-specific scans, marker suits, and person-specific training. There is no comparison to biomechanical simulation or other inverse anatomy methods under matched subject-specific inputs.

The model is person-specific and suit-dependent, with no validation on unseen subjects. The 'parametric model' contribution is therefore limited to five subject-specific networks rather than a generalizable anatomical human model.

Experimental details are insufficient for reproducibility: the train/validation split, definition of unseen poses, number of training frames, whether models are pooled or per-subject, and marker-failure handling are not clearly specified in the main paper.
Dataset ethics, consent, licensing, and privacy handling for releasing human scans, motion data, and demographics are not discussed, which is important for a human-centered dataset contribution.

There are minor technical/notational issues, e.g., E_data appears to omit a sum over time t while using N_t, and D_skin/D_musc notation is not always consistent, making the formulation harder to verify.

strengths: The paper addresses a novel and well-motivated ill-posed inverse problem: recovering internal muscle deformation directly from accessible multi-view RGB/surface observations, rather than relying on medical imaging or expensive FEM simulation. This is a meaningful step toward scalable biomechanical digital humans.

The SKIM dataset is a substantial contribution: five subjects, roughly 45 minutes of 120-camera capture per subject, a custom dense ArUco suit, high-resolution canonical skin/muscle/bone templates, marker trajectories, residual fields, and visibility masks. It fills a clear data gap for vision-based anatomical modeling.

The SOMA method is technically well-developed. It combines decoupled non-linear blendshapes for skin and muscle layers with biomechanically inspired priors (smoothness, bending resistance, stretch, tangential sliding, and prism-based volume preservation). The formulation is principled and goes beyond purely geometric soft-tissue models.

The experiments on unseen motions show clear gains in challenging dynamic regions. For example, the DRE >25 mm error is reduced to 64.52 mm versus 134.28 mm for LBS and 151.65 mm for HIT, and P90 tracking error is substantially lower than LBS. Subcutaneous volume distortion is also much lower than HIT in the S->M setting.
The individual-muscle propagation and interactive visualization framework are useful additions, enabling per-muscle inspection and animation-ready output in standard graphics engines.
The supplemental material provides extensive implementation details, data structure, hyperparameters, and derivations, which improves reproducibility and clarity.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering muscle deformation is not directly validated against internal volumetric ground truth. No dynamic in-vivo muscle measurements are available, and the internal anatomy is initialized from a template-fitting method. The evaluation therefore measures surface marker tracking, volume preservation, and collision avoidance rather than anatomical accuracy of the inferred muscles.

The skin/muscle decomposition is underdetermined. The muscle displacement field is supervised only indirectly through skin markers and separated from the skin residual via heuristic regularization weights. It is unclear whether the learned muscle motion corresponds to true underlying muscle behavior or merely a plausible regularized decomposition.

The method does not truly model independent individual muscle activations. High-resolution muscles are propagated from a single boundary muscle layer using barycentric transfer, so all muscles inherit the same deformation field. This limits claims about targeting individual muscles and cannot capture co-contraction or force variation at fixed pose.

The evaluation is person-specific and small-scale, covering only five subjects with no cross-subject generalization or demographic/body-shape analysis. The paper acknowledges this, but it remains an important limitation for a parametric-model contribution.

The main baseline, HIT, is a static internal-tissue estimator and not a dynamic muscle-deformation method. The comparison is informative but not fully matched, and no physics-based simulation or activation-based dynamic baseline is provided.

Some quantitative advantages are modest or mixed: MPME is slightly worse than LBS, deep muscle volume error is 10.35% versus HIT's 1.95%, and ablations occasionally differ by small margins. Statistical significance or per-subject variance is not reported.

The capture protocol relies on a tight ArUco marker suit and multi-view studio, which limits practical applicability and may introduce suit-skin slip or marker visibility issues. Visibility drops for target muscles such as biceps/brachialis at peak flexion could bias supervision exactly when bulging occurs.
Dataset release details such as licensing, subject consent, privacy handling, and explicit code/data links are not fully clear in the manuscript, which matters for a dataset contribution.
